objectives: Master the GATT/WTO system — eight rounds, MFN, national treatment, dispute settlement, Appellate Body crisis.
Survey post-WTO trade architecture — CPTPP, RCEP, USMCA, EU FTAs, the bilateral + plurilateral turn.
Master economic statecraft — sanctions, Hufbauer-Schott-Elliott methodology, export controls, financial weaponization, industrial policy.

slides.title: GATT → WTO: from 1947 Geneva to Doha + Appellate-Body crisis
slides.body:
**Economic + trade diplomacy** = the conduct of international economic relations through negotiation of trade + investment + monetary + financial agreements. The dominant diplomatic activity by volume in most foreign ministries — most state-to-state interactions touch on trade, investment, currency, sanctions, or commercial policy.

**Origins — Bretton Woods + the ITO**:
- **Bretton Woods Conference (July 1944)** — created the **IMF** + the **World Bank**. Cross-ref multilateral-institutions-and-un.
- **International Trade Organization (ITO)** — third Bretton Woods pillar, negotiated 1946-48 at the UN Conference on Trade + Employment (Havana 1947-48). The **Havana Charter** (Mar 1948) was ambitious — covering trade, employment, restrictive business practices, commodity agreements, investment. *U.S. Senate refused to ratify* (1950); ITO never came into being. The void was filled by the **General Agreement on Tariffs + Trade (GATT)**.

**The GATT (1947-1994)** — a 1947 *provisional* multilateral trade agreement signed by 23 contracting parties (Geneva 30 Oct 1947); applied *provisionally* under the Protocol of Provisional Application. Operated for 47 years as the *de facto* world trade organization through eight rounds of negotiation. Three core principles:

- **Most-Favored-Nation (MFN, GATT Art. I)** — any trade advantage granted to one contracting party must be extended *unconditionally* to all other contracting parties. The cornerstone of multilateral trade non-discrimination. Exceptions: FTAs + customs unions (Art. XXIV); GSP for developing countries (Enabling Clause 1979); regional integration; agriculture + textiles (historically); waivers.
- **National Treatment (GATT Art. III)** — imported products may not be treated less favorably than *like* domestic products in respect of internal taxation + regulation. Prevents border-tax substitution for tariffs + protects against disguised protectionism.
- **Tariff Bindings + Schedules of Concessions (GATT Art. II)** — each member submits a schedule of *bound* tariff rates (ceilings) which may not be raised without compensation. *Applied* rates may be below bound rates (*tariff water*).

**Other GATT principles**: transparency (Art. X); prohibition of quantitative restrictions (Art. XI — though heavily qualified); BoP exception (Art. XII); security exception (Art. XXI); general exceptions (Art. XX — public morals, human/animal/plant life or health, exhaustible natural resources, etc.).

**The eight GATT rounds** — successive multilateral tariff + rule-making negotiations:
1. **Geneva 1947** — 23 countries; ~45000 tariff concessions on ~$10B of trade; founded the GATT.
2. **Annecy 1949** — 13 countries.
3. **Torquay 1950-51** — 38 countries.
4. **Geneva 1955-56** — 26 countries.
5. **Dillon Round 1960-61** — 26 countries; named after U.S. Treasury Secretary C. Douglas Dillon.
6. **Kennedy Round 1964-67** — 62 countries; first negotiation of *across-the-board* tariff cuts (35% average); anti-dumping code.
7. **Tokyo Round 1973-79** — 102 countries; non-tariff measures (codes on subsidies, anti-dumping, customs valuation, government procurement, standards, import licensing); GSP enabling clause (1979). The first round to address NTMs systematically.
8. **Uruguay Round 1986-94** — 123 countries; the most ambitious round in history. Outcomes:
   - **Marrakesh Agreement (Apr 1994)** establishing the **World Trade Organization (WTO)** — entered into force 1 January 1995.
   - **GATT 1994** — updated tariff agreements.
   - **General Agreement on Trade in Services (GATS)** — first multilateral disciplines on services trade.
   - **TRIPS** — Trade-Related Aspects of Intellectual Property Rights — minimum IP standards.
   - **Agreement on Agriculture** — first time agriculture brought fully under multilateral disciplines.
   - **Agreement on Subsidies + Countervailing Measures (SCM)**, **Anti-Dumping Agreement**, **TBT** (technical barriers), **SPS** (sanitary + phytosanitary), **TRIMs**, **Safeguards**, **Plurilateral Agreement on Government Procurement (GPA)**, **Civil Aircraft**.
   - **Dispute Settlement Understanding (DSU)** — *the WTO's crown jewel*; binding adjudication; Appellate Body; reverse-consensus adoption.
   - **Trade Policy Review Mechanism (TPRM)** — periodic peer review.

**The WTO (1995-)** — Geneva HQ; 164 members + 25 observers; Marrakesh Agreement as the constituent treaty. **Director-Generals** — Renato Ruggiero (Italy 1995-99), Mike Moore (NZ 1999-2002), Supachai Panitchpakdi (Thailand 2002-05), Pascal Lamy (France 2005-13), Roberto Azevêdo (Brazil 2013-20), Ngozi Okonjo-Iweala (Nigeria 2021-). Decision-making by consensus; Ministerial Conferences every two years (MC1 Singapore 1996 → MC13 Abu Dhabi 2024).

**Dispute Settlement Body (DSB) + the Appellate Body** — the WTO's adjudicatory machinery. Members file complaints; consultations; panel established; panel report; appeal to *Appellate Body* (7 members; legal review); DSB adoption by *reverse consensus* (the report is adopted unless ALL members agree NOT to adopt — a near-impossibility). Compliance + retaliation procedures (Art. 22 DSU). Over 600 disputes filed (1995-2024); landmark cases — *Shrimp-Turtle* (1998), *EC-Hormones* (1998), *US-Cotton* (2005), *China-Rare Earths* (2014), *Boeing-Airbus* (2004-2020 saga), *China-IP* (2009).

**The Appellate Body crisis (2017-2019+)**. The Trump administration began blocking new Appellate Body appointments in 2017 + by Dec 2019 the AB lacked the three members required for quorum + ceased functioning. U.S. complaints: judicial overreach, Member-State sovereignty erosion, 90-day deadlines routinely missed, retroactive interpretation. Workarounds: **Multi-Party Interim Appeal Arbitration Arrangement (MPIA)** under DSU Art. 25 — EU + China + Australia + Canada + 25+ others have agreed to interim arbitration pending AB restoration. AB restoration has been ongoing as the 2025 negotiation agenda — no resolution by MC13 (Feb 2024) or expected by mid-2025.

**Doha Development Round (launched Nov 2001 at Doha MC)** — the WTO's first round. *Single undertaking* across agriculture, NAMA (non-agricultural market access), services, rules, IP, environment, development. Effectively *stalled* since the July 2008 Geneva mini-ministerial collapse — fundamental disagreement among U.S. + EU (subsidies + tariffs in agriculture), India + China (special safeguards for developing countries), Brazil + the G20 trade group (developing-country agriculture access). MC9 Bali 2013 + MC10 Nairobi 2015 produced narrow agreements (Trade Facilitation Agreement; export-competition agriculture decisions) but no comprehensive package. Effectively dead by MC11 Buenos Aires 2017.

**Post-Doha plurilateral + bilateral turn** — major trade liberalization has shifted to:
- **Comprehensive + Progressive Agreement for Trans-Pacific Partnership (CPTPP, 2018)** — 11 countries (post-U.S. withdrawal from TPP in 2017); UK acceded 2024; high-standard FTA covering goods + services + investment + IP + digital + labor + environment + SOEs.
- **Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership (RCEP, 2020)** — 15 countries (ASEAN + China + Japan + ROK + Australia + NZ); the world's largest FTA by GDP coverage; lower standards than CPTPP but broader Asian coverage.
- **United States-Mexico-Canada Agreement (USMCA, 2020)** — successor to NAFTA (1994); higher labor + auto + IP standards.
- **EU Free Trade Agreements** — EU-Japan EPA (2019), EU-Vietnam (2020), EU-Mercosur (negotiated 2019, ratified 2024), EU-Canada CETA (2017), EU-UK Trade + Cooperation Agreement (2020).
- **African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA, 2018)** — 54 African Union members; ambitious continent-wide market integration; operational from 2021.
- **Indo-Pacific Economic Framework (IPEF, 2022)** — Biden-era U.S. initiative; 14 countries; *non-tariff* framework covering trade, supply chains, clean economy, anti-corruption. Trump-administration retrenchment 2025.

**Plurilateral initiatives at WTO** — Joint Statement Initiatives on e-commerce (88 members; concluded 2024), services domestic regulation (concluded 2021), investment facilitation (concluded 2023), MSMEs, gender + trade — *clubs within the club* approach to revive multilateralism.

slides.title: Sanctions: Hufbauer-Schott-Elliott + the modern sanctions revolution
slides.body:
**Sanctions** = coercive economic measures imposed by one state, group of states, or international organization on a target state, entity, or individual to compel changes in policy or behavior. The dominant tool of *coercive economic statecraft* in the 21st century — vastly expanded in scope + sophistication since the 1990s.

**Foundational scholarship — Gary Clyde Hufbauer + Jeffrey Schott + Kimberly Ann Elliott — *Economic Sanctions Reconsidered*** (PIIE/IIE; first ed. 1985; 2nd ed. 1990; 3rd ed. 2007 + 2009 supplement with Barbara Oegg). The definitive empirical work on sanctions effectiveness.
- **Methodology**: coded 174 sanctions episodes 1914-2000 across multiple dimensions — sender(s), target, goal, type, costs, side effects, success.
- **Headline finding**: sanctions *succeed* in achieving at least part of their stated policy goals in approximately **34%** of cases — but success defined broadly; *fully achieved goals + dominant causal role* is much rarer (~10-15%).
- **Success-correlates**: (a) modest policy goals; (b) target politically + economically weak relative to sender; (c) sanctions imposed swiftly + decisively; (d) target friendly or formerly friendly to sender; (e) low costs to sender; (f) absence of major third-party sanctions-busters. (g) High-leverage *senders* (U.S., EU, UN).
- **Failure-correlates**: ambitious goals (regime change, destabilization); strong/large targets; gradual escalation that allows adaptation; targets with diversification options; major third-party assistance.
- **The Hufbauer-Schott-Elliott (HSE) database + scoring methodology** is the standard reference. Critics (Robert Pape *International Security* 1997 — 'Why Economic Sanctions Do Not Work'; Daniel Drezner + various) debate the methodology + finding.

**Daniel Drezner — *The Sanctions Paradox*** (1999) + *The Politics of Persuasion* (2003) + numerous *Foreign Affairs* + scholarly essays. Drezner's signaling-+-bargaining framework: sanctions function partly to *signal* resolve to domestic + allied audiences + secondarily to coerce target.

**Sanctions types**:
- **Comprehensive sanctions** — broad embargoes on trade + finance with the target country. Historical: Cuba (1960-), Iraq (1990-2003), North Korea (2006-), Iran (1979-2016 + 2018-). Heavy humanitarian costs + collateral damage; mostly replaced by targeted sanctions since the late 1990s.
- **Smart / targeted sanctions** — *Interlaken Process* (1998-99), *Bonn-Berlin Process* (1999-2001), *Stockholm Process* (2001-03) — multilateral expert processes that shifted UN + national practice toward sanctions on *specific individuals + entities* rather than entire economies. Asset freezes, travel bans, financial-network restrictions, sectoral measures (oil, banking, defense).
- **Sectoral sanctions** — restrictions on specific sectors (Russian oil + gas + financial; Iranian oil + central bank; Venezuelan oil; Belarusian potash).
- **Secondary sanctions** — penalties on third-country actors that transact with primary-sanctions targets. U.S. innovations leveraging dollar hegemony (Iran 2010+; North Korea; Russia 2022+; ICC officials 2020, 2025).
- **Financial / dollar-clearing sanctions** — exclusion from U.S. financial system + SWIFT; *de facto* exclusion from international finance.
- **Export controls** — restrictions on outbound technology transfer; Wassenaar Arrangement (1996+) successor to COCOM; U.S. Export Administration Regulations (EAR) + CFIUS + Entity List + Foreign Direct Product Rule. Cross-ref chip controls in modern-frontier-diplomacy.

**UN sanctions** — Chapter VII Art. 41 measures. Currently active regimes: ISIL/Al-Qaeda (1267/1989/2253); Taliban (1988); DPRK (1718/1874/2087/2094/2270/2321/2371/2375/2397); Iran (now lifted via JCPOA-related dynamics; UN Iran sanctions terminated 2025 by snapback dispute); Libya (1970); Sudan; CAR; Somalia; Yemen; Mali (terminated 2023); DRC. Sanctions committees + monitoring panels + experts panels.

**EU sanctions** — Common Foreign + Security Policy (CFSP) regime; >40 sanctions programs; major regimes — Russia (2014+, dramatically expanded 2022+), Iran, Belarus, Syria, Myanmar, Venezuela, North Korea, ISIL/Al-Qaeda. EU Global Human Rights Sanctions Regime (2020) — Magnitsky-style framework.

**U.S. sanctions** — OFAC (Office of Foreign Assets Control, Treasury) administers ~30+ sanctions programs covering ~12000 entities + individuals. *Specially Designated Nationals (SDN)* list. Legal authorities — International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA 1977), Trading with the Enemy Act, country-specific statutes, Magnitsky Act (2012) + Global Magnitsky (2016) + Hong Kong Human Rights + Democracy Act (2019).

**The Russia sanctions package (2022+)** — most comprehensive sanctions ever imposed on a major economy.
- *Russian central bank reserves frozen* (~$300B; G7 + EU action Feb 2022); historic precedent.
- *SWIFT exclusion* of major Russian banks (Feb-Mar 2022).
- *Oil price cap* (Dec 2022) — G7 + EU + Australia $60/bbl cap on Russian crude shipped using G7+ insurance + services; novel mechanism balancing price suppression + supply preservation.
- *Export controls* — Foreign Direct Product Rule extended to Russia; chip + dual-use technology restrictions.
- *14 EU sanctions packages* + multiple U.S. + UK + Japanese + Korean + Australian + Canadian + NZ + Singapore measures.
- *Effectiveness debate* — Russian economy contracted modestly in 2022, recovered 2023-24 on military spending + sanctions evasion via parallel imports + crypto + UAE + Turkey + China trade. Long-run sectoral damage substantial; macro damage less than predicted.

**Sanctions evasion + circumvention** — *parallel imports*; *ghost shipping* (Russian shadow fleet 2022+); cryptocurrency (Tornado Cash, mixers); offshore + shell companies; *secondary-market dollar systems* (PSE Petro-yuan, BRICS Pay).

**Humanitarian impact + critiques**:
- **Joy Gordon — *Invisible War* (2010)** + sanctions on Iraq + UNICEF estimates of child mortality.
- **Idriss Jazairy — UN Special Rapporteur on the negative impact of unilateral coercive measures**.
- **Cuba + Iran + North Korea + Venezuela** sanctions humanitarian-impact debates.
- **Carve-outs + humanitarian licenses** — recent UN + U.S. + EU practice to permit humanitarian transactions.

**Magnitsky regime + human-rights sanctions** — Sergei Magnitsky's death in Russian custody (2009) → U.S. Magnitsky Act (2012) → Global Magnitsky Act (2016) — sanctions on individuals worldwide for human-rights abuses + corruption. *Magnitsky-style* legislation now in UK (2018 SAMLA + 2020 Global Human Rights Sanctions Regulations), EU (2020), Canada (2017), Australia (2021), Japan (de facto), New Zealand. Used against PRC Xinjiang officials (2020+), Russian + Belarusian officials, Saudi MBS associates (Khashoggi), Iranian morality-police officials (2022+).

**Industrial policy + state aid + subsidies**:
- **CHIPS + Science Act (U.S. 2022)** — $52B semiconductor subsidies + R&D + workforce.
- **Inflation Reduction Act (U.S. 2022)** — ~$370B clean-energy + climate subsidies with Buy American provisions; sparked EU + Korea + Japan trade tensions.
- **EU Chips Act (2023)** + **EU Green Deal Industrial Plan**.
- **Made in China 2025** (2015 onward; less publicly emphasized after 2018 trade war) + dual circulation strategy.
- **WTO Subsidies + Countervailing Measures Agreement** strain — major economies increasingly using *prohibited* + *actionable* subsidies; reform debate.

**Bremmer's *The End of the Free World*** (2020) + *Every Nation for Itself* (2012) — the global political-risk + sanctions environment in the *G-Zero* era.

**Henry Farrell + Abraham Newman — *Underground Empire*** (2023) + *Chained to Globalization* (2021) — *weaponized interdependence* — networks of financial + technological + supply-chain interdependence become coercive instruments in the hands of states that control key chokepoints (U.S. dollar clearing + cloud computing + semiconductor design; China rare earths + manufacturing; Taiwan TSMC; Netherlands ASML).

slides.title: Trade negotiation practice + the future of economic diplomacy
slides.body:
**The trade negotiator's craft** — how trade agreements are actually negotiated.

**Pre-negotiation phase**:
- **Scoping + feasibility studies** — joint study groups, sectoral consultations, modeling (CGE — Computable General Equilibrium — models from Purdue GTAP, World Bank, USITC).
- **Stakeholder consultation** — domestic industry, agriculture, labor, environment, indigenous groups, sub-national governments.
- **Mandate + negotiating directives** — domestic political authorization (Trade Promotion Authority in U.S.; EU Council mandate; Diet authorization in Japan).
- **Chief negotiator + delegation** — lead trade ministry official + sectoral experts + lawyers + economists.

**Negotiation phase**:
- **Chapter-by-chapter negotiation** — typically 25-30 chapters covering: national treatment + market access for goods; rules of origin; customs + trade facilitation; SPS; TBT; trade remedies; services; investment; financial services; telecoms; e-commerce; government procurement; IP; competition; SOEs; SMEs; labor; environment; gender; transparency + anti-corruption; dispute settlement; institutional + final provisions.
- **Negotiating texts** — *consolidated text* with bracketed alternatives; *clean text* once consensus reached on each provision.
- **Market access negotiations** — *request-offer* tariff lines; rules of origin (RVC — regional value content); services schedules (positive vs negative list).
- **Side letters + understandings** — bilateral clarifications + sensitive provisions.
- **Endgame** — *political conclusion* at ministerial or leader level; lawyer-linguist review; signature.

**Post-negotiation**:
- **Ratification** — U.S. Congress implementing legislation; EU Parliament + member-state ratification for mixed agreements; varying processes elsewhere.
- **Implementation** — domestic regulatory transposition; customs procedures; certificate-of-origin systems.
- **Joint committees + working groups** — ongoing implementation oversight.
- **Dispute settlement** — bilateral panels + WTO + ISDS + state-state.

**Investor-State Dispute Settlement (ISDS)** — investor-state arbitration provisions in BITs + investment chapters of FTAs. ICSID (Convention 1965; ~900 cases) + UNCITRAL + ICC + ad hoc tribunals.
- *Major cases* — Argentine emergency-measures cases (2001-02 crisis, ~50 BIT cases); *Philip Morris v. Australia* (2016 tobacco plain-packaging, jurisdiction denied); *Vattenfall v. Germany* (nuclear phase-out, settled).
- **ISDS reform** — UNCITRAL Working Group III ongoing reforms; *Investment Court System (ICS)* in EU FTAs (Canada CETA, Vietnam); proposed *Multilateral Investment Court (MIC)*; the *backlash* of South Africa, India, Indonesia, Bolivia, Venezuela withdrawing from BITs + ICSID.

**The bilateral + plurilateral + 'mini-lateral' turn**:
- **CPTPP, RCEP, USMCA, EU FTAs, AfCFTA, IPEF** (previous slide).
- **Indo-Pacific Economic Framework (IPEF, 2022)** — Biden-era 14-country framework; 4 pillars (trade, supply chains, clean economy, fair economy); concluded 3 of 4 pillars 2023-24; trade pillar incomplete; *Trump 2025 retrenchment*.
- **Climate Club + Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM)** — EU CBAM (transition 2023-26; full 2026+); pressure for *climate-aligned* trade architecture; G7 Climate Club.
- **Critical-minerals + supply-chain agreements** — U.S.-Japan Critical Minerals Agreement (2023); U.S.-EU Critical Raw Materials Club; mutual-recognition for IRA EV-credit eligibility.

**The U.S.-China trade conflict (2018-)**:
- **2018 Trump tariffs** — Section 301 tariffs on ~$370B of Chinese imports (avg ~19%); 232 steel + aluminum tariffs.
- **2020 Phase One deal** — Liu He + Lighthizer + Mnuchin; $200B Chinese purchase commitments (largely unmet); IP commitments.
- **Biden 2021-24** — preserved most Trump tariffs; added strategic export controls (advanced AI chips Oct 2022 + Oct 2023 updates); outbound investment screening (2023+); IRA + CHIPS Act competitive industrial policy.
- **Trump 2025+** — *reciprocal tariff* regime; 10-25%+ baseline; sectoral + country-specific add-ons; broad scope including allies; trade-policy as primary leverage instrument.

**Currency + monetary diplomacy** — the IMF's domain + central-bank diplomacy.
- **G7 + G20 finance** — monetary cooperation; FX coordination (Plaza Accord 1985 strengthening yen + DM; Louvre Accord 1987).
- **Swap lines** — Fed + ECB + BoE + BoJ + SNB + BoC standing arrangements; emerging-market crisis lending.
- **CBDC + payments diplomacy** — mBridge multi-CBDC, BIS Innovation Hub, *Project Agorá*; the future of cross-border payments; geopolitical dollar-vs-non-dollar competition.

**Climate + environmental diplomacy intersection**:
- **Paris Agreement (2015)** + NDCs + climate finance — $100B/yr commitment + $300B/yr 2024 NCQG.
- **CBAM + climate-related trade measures** — EU 2023+; growing G7 + South divergence.
- **Loss + damage fund** (COP27 2022).
- Cross-ref modern-frontier-diplomacy on Paris + carbon-border + global stocktake.

**Development + aid diplomacy**:
- **OECD Development Assistance Committee (DAC)** + ODA reporting (~$240B 2023; ~0.37% DAC GNI; UN target 0.7%).
- **Multilateral development banks** — World Bank + IFAD + ADB + AfDB + IADB + EIB + EBRD + AIIB (China-founded 2016) + NDB (BRICS Bank 2014).
- **Belt + Road Initiative (BRI, 2013+)** — China's grand-strategic infrastructure + financing initiative; ~150+ countries; ~$1T+ committed; major leverage instrument.
- **U.S. *Build Back Better World* (B3W 2021) → Partnership for Global Infrastructure + Investment (PGII)** — Western response; ~$600B over 5 years committed.
- **EU Global Gateway (2021)** — €300B mobilized 2021-27.

**Trade-bloc futures**:
- **CPTPP enlargement** — UK 2024; pending applications from China, Taiwan, Ecuador, Costa Rica, Uruguay.
- **RCEP deepening + ASEAN-centrality** — ongoing.
- **AfCFTA implementation** — protocols on investment, IP, e-commerce, women + youth; full implementation expected 2030s.
- **WTO reform agenda** — Appellate Body restoration; rule-making on subsidies, fisheries (concluded 2022 Pesca; phase 2 ongoing), digital trade, climate, gender.

**Economic statecraft in 2025** — the world has shifted from *liberal trade integration* (1995-2018) to *managed competition + decoupling-derisking* (2018-) to *strategic decoupling + great-power tariff competition* (2025+).
- *Geoeconomic regionalism* — Indo-Pacific, EU, North America, BRICS+, GCC, regional African + Latin American integration.
- *Industrial policy renaissance* — Inflation Reduction Act + CHIPS Act + EU Green Deal + Chinese state-owned-enterprise enhancements.
- *Weaponized interdependence* (Farrell + Newman) — chokepoint sanctions + export controls + financial restrictions as primary coercive instruments.
- *Allied coalitions + economic NATO* — G7 + Quad + IPEF + AUKUS commercial dimensions.

The trade diplomat in 2025 must navigate WTO law + multiple FTA regimes + bilateral negotiations + sanctions compliance + export controls + industrial-policy provisions + climate-trade measures + technology restrictions — a vastly more complex landscape than the WTO's high-water mark in 2001.

question.question: Apply Hufbauer-Schott-Elliott methodology to assess a sanctions program
question.goal: A coalition of states (the *senders*) considers comprehensive financial + export-control sanctions against country X over X's nuclear-weapons program. Apply Hufbauer-Schott-Elliott methodology to predict success likelihood + design.

steps.prompt: What are HSE's main success-correlates + how do they apply here?

acceptedAnswers: hse success factors include modest policy goals weak target relative to senders swift decisive imposition friendly or formerly friendly target low cost to sender absence of major third party sanctions busters and high leverage senders nuclear nonproliferation is an ambitious goal so success is harder

steps.reveal: HSE's empirical success-correlates: (a) **modest goals** — sanctions succeed more often at minor policy changes than at regime change or major-strategic-program reversal. *Nuclear-weapons-program rollback is among the most ambitious goals* (success rates historically very low — ~10-15%). (b) **Weak target** — X's economic + political resilience matters; small + import-dependent + financially-vulnerable economies sanction more easily. (c) **Swift + decisive imposition** — gradual escalation lets target adapt. (d) **Friendly or formerly friendly target** — political openness to bargaining. (e) **Low cost to sender** — sender resolve. (f) **No major third-party busters** — closing off Russia + China + UAE + Turkey + Iran circumvention is essential. (g) **High-leverage senders** — U.S. + EU + UK + Japan + ROK + Australia. The nuclear-rollback goal places this case in the *hardest* success category.

steps.prompt: How should the program be designed for maximum impact?

acceptedAnswers: comprehensive financial sanctions targeting central bank reserves swift exclusion and dollar clearing sectoral oil and trade restrictions targeted sanctions on regime elites secondary sanctions on third country circumventers export controls on dual use technology and an explicit off ramp tied to verifiable rollback steps

steps.reveal: **Design recommendations**: (1) **Comprehensive financial sanctions** — freeze central bank + sovereign-wealth-fund assets (precedent: Russia Feb 2022); SWIFT exclusion of major banks; dollar-clearing restrictions. (2) **Sectoral sanctions** — oil + gas + petrochemicals + dual-use industrial; *oil price cap* mechanism (precedent: G7 Russia Dec 2022) to preserve supply but suppress price. (3) **Targeted sanctions on regime elites** — Magnitsky-style sanctions on leadership + IRGC-equivalents + family financial networks. (4) **Secondary sanctions** — penalties on third-country actors transacting with X (Iran precedent). (5) **Export controls** — Foreign Direct Product Rule + Entity List for dual-use + chip + missile-related items. (6) **Off-ramps + clear conditions** — specific + verifiable nuclear-rollback steps tied to sanctions relief — *JCPOA template*. Without credible off-ramps, sanctions become *forever sanctions* + lose leverage. The *condition + relief sequencing* is the negotiator's lever.

steps.prompt: What are the main risks + side-effects?

acceptedAnswers: humanitarian harm to civilians driving anti sender backlash sanctions busting through china russia uae turkey adaptation and resilience through import substitution and parallel financial systems escalation risk pushing toward military confrontation reduced future negotiation flexibility and erosion of sanctions effectiveness through over use

hints: Humanitarian; busting; adaptation; escalation; future leverage.
steps.reveal: **Main risks**: (1) **Humanitarian harm** — Joy Gordon *Invisible War* on Iraq 1990s; child mortality + medical supply effects; backlash domestically + internationally; carve-outs + licenses essential. (2) **Sanctions-busting** — third-country circumvention via China + Russia + UAE + Turkey + Iran + others; parallel financial systems (CIPS + SPFS + BRICS Pay + crypto). (3) **Target adaptation** — import substitution + parallel-import + state-led financial restructuring; the Russian + Iranian + DPRK precedents show targets can adapt to comprehensive sanctions over years. (4) **Escalation risk** — comprehensive sanctions can push targets toward military confrontation rather than concession (1941 Japanese precedent often cited). (5) **Reduced future leverage** — over-use erodes credibility + accelerates de-dollarization + parallel-system development (cross-ref Farrell + Newman *Underground Empire* 2023). (6) **Allied coordination** — fragmentation between U.S. + EU + Japan + ROK can let X exploit divergences. *Sanctions design must address each risk explicitly*.

steps.prompt: What does this imply for diplomatic strategy?

acceptedAnswers: sanctions are most effective when paired with active diplomacy backchannels and credible incentives so the strategy should integrate maximum pressure with sustained diplomatic engagement clear off ramps allied coordination and willingness to provide reciprocal commitments tied to verifiable rollback steps

steps.reveal: **Strategic implications**: sanctions are most effective when *paired with active diplomacy* — they are leverage, not substitute for negotiation. (1) **Maintain backchannels** — quiet diplomatic engagement throughout sanctions imposition (JCPOA + Iran + DPRK + Cuba precedents). (2) **Credible off-ramps** — clear + verifiable rollback steps with specific sanctions relief; *step-for-step reciprocity*. (3) **Sustain allied coordination** — G7 + EU + Japan + ROK + Australia + NZ + others; coalition discipline. (4) **Manage third-party defection** — engage China + India + UAE on enforcement; targeted secondary sanctions where needed. (5) **Plan for negotiated outcome** — sanctions should serve a *political theory of victory* — what does success look like? Without that, sanctions become a default *forever* response. *Combine pressure + diplomacy + credible exit* is the canonical model (JCPOA 2015 template + lessons from its 2018 collapse).

question.question: Why is the WTO Most-Favored-Nation principle (GATT Art. I) the cornerstone of the multilateral trading system?
options: Most-Favored-Nation (GATT Art. I; WTO Marrakesh 1995) requires that any trade advantage granted to one contracting party must be extended *unconditionally + immediately* to all other WTO members. The principle institutionalizes *non-discrimination* + *multilateralism* — it converts every bilateral concession into a multilateral public good. Three reasons it is the cornerstone: (1) **Non-discrimination** — protects smaller members from being systematically disadvantaged by power-political bilateral deals among great powers; the original 1947 GATT bargain made U.S.-UK-France-Canada concessions automatically available to all signatories. (2) **Incentive alignment** — converts the trade negotiation from zero-sum bilateral haggling into multilateral cooperative bargaining; the Geneva → Tokyo → Uruguay rounds each succeeded because MFN multiplied concessions. (3) **Predictability + transparency** — members + traders know that any concession is permanent + universal; reduces transaction costs + risk. Exceptions: FTAs + customs unions (Art. XXIV; CPTPP, RCEP, USMCA, EU FTAs); GSP (Enabling Clause 1979); security exceptions (Art. XXI). The post-Doha era has stressed MFN as bilateral + plurilateral agreements proliferate + as Trump-era 'reciprocal tariffs' explicitly reject MFN, but MFN remains the constitutional anchor of multilateral trade.
question.explanation: MFN (GATT Art. I; WTO 1995) requires any trade advantage granted to one WTO member extends unconditionally + immediately to all others. (1) Non-discrimination protects smaller members. (2) Incentive alignment converts bilateral concessions into multilateral cooperative bargaining — drove successive GATT rounds. (3) Predictability + transparency. Exceptions: FTAs + customs unions Art. XXIV; GSP Enabling Clause 1979; security Art. XXI. Stressed by FTA proliferation + Trump 'reciprocal tariffs' but remains constitutional anchor of multilateral trade.

hints: What does it require + what are the exceptions?
slides.workedSolution: MFN (GATT Art. I; WTO 1995) — any trade advantage to one member extends unconditionally to all. Non-discrimination + incentive alignment for multilateral cooperation + predictability. Exceptions: FTAs/customs unions Art. XXIV; GSP Enabling Clause; security Art. XXI. Constitutional anchor of multilateral trade despite FTA proliferation + recent reciprocal-tariff challenges.

question.question: Design a coordinated allied response to economic coercion
question.prompt: Country Y has imposed informal trade restrictions on country A's exports (selective customs delays, regulatory harassment, unofficial import bans) in retaliation for A's diplomatic positions on human rights. You advise A's foreign minister. Write a ≤220-word strategic memo applying (a) WTO law (MFN, national treatment, NTM disciplines, DSB) — assess whether a WTO complaint is viable; (b) Hufbauer-Schott-Elliott + Drezner sanctions/coercion analytics — likely Y leverage + A's BATNA; (c) plurilateral coalition design — possible cooperation with EU + Japan + ROK + Australia + Canada on coordinated response; (d) economic-statecraft toolkit — export controls, anti-coercion instruments (EU ACI 2023), import diversification, supply-chain resilience, public communication; (e) integrate Farrell + Newman *weaponized interdependence* + Bremmer *G-Zero* framing. Recommend a specific 3-track response (legal, economic, diplomatic) + identify the main political + economic costs to A.

question.question: Hufbauer-Schott-Elliott (2007) report sanctions success in approximately $S = 34\%$ of $N = 174$ episodes (1914-2000). Compute the approximate number of *successful* episodes $N_S = S \cdot N = 0.34 \cdot 174$, rounded to the nearest integer.
question.hint: $N_S = 0.34 \cdot 174 \approx 59.16 \approx 59$ episodes. HSE's 34% success rate is *partially* successful by their broad definition; *fully achieved goals + dominant causal role* is much rarer (~10-15%; ~17-26 episodes). HSE methodology (1985, 1990, 2007 with Oegg) remains the canonical empirical reference + is debated by Pape *International Security* 1997, Drezner *The Sanctions Paradox* 1999, + ongoing scholarship.

question.prompt: In ≤140 words, integrate (a) the GATT/WTO system — eight rounds + MFN + national treatment + DSB + Appellate Body crisis + Doha stalemate; (b) post-Doha bilateral + plurilateral architecture — CPTPP + RCEP + USMCA + EU FTAs + AfCFTA + IPEF; (c) economic statecraft — Hufbauer + Schott + Elliott sanctions methodology + Drezner + Farrell + Newman weaponized interdependence; + (d) the 2018+ shift from liberal integration to strategic competition + decoupling + tariff competition.
question.rubric: Mentions: **GATT/WTO** — GATT 1947 with MFN (Art. I) + national treatment (Art. III) + tariff bindings (Art. II); eight rounds (Geneva → Annecy → Torquay → Geneva → Dillon → Kennedy → Tokyo → Uruguay) culminating in Marrakesh 1994 + WTO 1995 with GATS + TRIPS + DSU + Appellate Body; 164 members. **Appellate Body crisis** since Trump blocked appointments 2017; MPIA (DSU Art. 25) workaround. **Doha** launched 2001; effectively stalled since 2008; MC9 Bali 2013 + MC10 Nairobi 2015 partial deliverables; effectively dead by MC11 2017. **Post-Doha architecture** — CPTPP 2018 (11 → 12 with UK 2024); RCEP 2020 (15 countries); USMCA 2020; EU FTAs (Japan, Vietnam, Mercosur, Canada CETA, UK TCA); AfCFTA 2018; IPEF 2022. **Sanctions** — **Hufbauer + Schott + Elliott** *Economic Sanctions Reconsidered* (1985/1990/2007) with 34% success rate on 174 episodes; Pape critique 1997; Drezner *Sanctions Paradox* 1999; smart sanctions (Interlaken + Bonn-Berlin + Stockholm processes 1998-2003); Magnitsky + Global Magnitsky 2012/2016; Russia 2022+ package (CB reserves freeze + SWIFT + oil price cap + FDPR); Farrell + Newman *Underground Empire* 2023 weaponized interdependence; Bremmer *G-Zero*. **2018+ shift** — Trump 301 + 232 tariffs; Biden export controls (chip Oct 2022 + 2023); industrial policy (CHIPS + IRA + EU Chips Act + Green Deal); Trump 2025 reciprocal tariffs; strategic decoupling + derisking. Concludes that economic + trade diplomacy has shifted from liberal-integration paradigm (1995-2018) to managed-competition + strategic-rivalry paradigm (2018-).
